newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban claim new advances in Kapisa province.
newsitem.headline: Taleban claim new advances in Kapisa province.

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia said it had captured parts of Kapisa province, northwest of Kabul, from opposition forces on Friday.
Taleban-controlled Voice of Sharia radio also said that a Taleban fighter had shot down a warplane of the opposition alliance with a U.S.-made Stinger anti-aircraft missile.
The radio said the Taleban had seized several towns and villages in Kapisa, including the provincial capital Mahmoud Raki, capturing large amounts of ammunition.

It gave no word on casualties, but sources quoted by the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press said that at least three soldiers of former government commander Ahmad Shah Masood had been killed and five Taleban fighters wounded in the fighting.

The radio said an opposition jet, apparently intending to bomb Charikar, a town captured by the Taleban on Thursday, was shot down in flames at midday. The aircraft, with the pilot still inside, fell on a mountainside.
It said the plane had been downed by a fighter commanded by Mullah Salam Rocketi, famed for his skill with Stingers during the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s.
No independent confirmation of the shooting down, or of the fighting in Kapisa province, was available.

The Taleban pushed forces loyal to Masood and his ally, northern Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum, out of Charikar and seized the big Soviet-built airbase of Bagram in a dawn attack on Thursday that apparently met little resistance.

Taleban fighters and travellers interviewed on Friday at this village, 30 km (19 miles) south of Bagram, said there had been little overnight fighting and the front line had moved two km (one mile) north of Charikar, now largely deserted.
Taleban's bearded fighters were in full control of Bagram airbase and celebrating with bursts of fire from assault rifles and machineguns, witnesses said.
The base, on a dusty plain with snow-capped peaks in the background, was used by Soviet forces in the 1980s to support a communist-backed government in Kabul.
Military analysts said the latest Taleban victory was a significant lift for the purist Islamic movement's morale but had not necessarily dealt the opposition alliance a killer blow.

Masood, forced to flee to his native Panjsher Valley after the Taleban seized Kabul on September 27, used guerrilla tactics successfully during a fightback in October that brought his forces back to within 20 km (13 miles) of the capital.
He helped the well-armed, mainly ethnic Tajik population of the Shomali Valley to mount ambushes against the Taleban from villages, vineyards and orchards along the road to the north.

But forces loyal to Masood and his rival-turned-ally General Abdul Rashid Dostum failed to break through Taleban defences around Kabul, just as the Islamic warriors had earlier failed to penetrate Dostum's northern heartland beyond the Hindu Kush mountain range or Masood's Panjsher redoubt.
Military analysts said it would be harder now for Masood to mobilise armed civilians against the Taleban in the Shomali Valley, partly because so many have now fled the area.
"I wouldn't place too many bets on a new uprising, but Masood is a master of guerrilla operations," one said.
The Taleban, seeking to impose their strict brand of Islam on Afghanistan, took the offensive one day after U.N.-sponsored peace talks ended inconclusively in Islamabad.
The Taleban now control up to three-quarters of Afghanistan, but have found it hard to consolidate their hold on areas outside their mainly Pashtun native provinces in the south.
